topics.title: A miscellaneous Countdown round question
topics.text:
Hi all,

Here's something I just thought of: what happens if they run out of Countdown questions at Mathcounts Nationals? Since CDR is official at Nats, if they exhaust all 80 questions with neither person getting 4 right in a matchup in the finals, what do they do then? Clearly they can't just not decide a national champion. :P



If one person's ahead, they'll probably just make that person the champion, but what if both are tied after question 80? What if they're both tied with zero?



(Of course, they may just take whoever's the higher written seed as the winner, but I can't confirm this anywhere.)



Just curious - this just occurred to me now. :)

topics.title: 1st Annual AoPS Mathematics Competition, Fall 2017
topics.text:
IMAGE



To start off, I decided that we should create a continued annual competition, right when school starts, since many people are active. This year is the first year of the Annual AoPS Mathematics Competition, so I want it to be a good one! Also, there will be different AoPS users, depending on votes, hosting this competition each year. Also, the creators of this competition are not AoPS administrators, they are also users. The tests have been released on our website: http://aopsm.weebly.com/take-the-test-now.html. The competition is not very long, but will have tiebreaking procedures, such as sudden death, where two people have the same score, but one of them gets an earlier question in the Marathon Round incorrect, they get the lower placement. Results will be announced in early December, and the competition begins on November 2nd. You must register before taking the test; the form for this is also in our website: http://aopsm.weebly.com/register.html. From now on, there is no discussion of the AAMC that can occur, such as test content. Any such activity found will resort to an automatic ban or removal from any AoPS Math Club activity or AAMC competition. The highest scores in each category will be rewarded, the overall highest score will be commended and given a special merit certificate. Thank you for participating and good luck!



INSTRUCTIONS

This contest features 5 rounds:

$\cdot$ Marathon Round - (15 questions, 30 minutes, 2 pts per question correct, -1 pts per incorrect, 0 pts per skipped) (Short Answer) (range from MC Chapter - MC National)

$\cdot$ Bull’s Eye! Round - (4 questions, 20 minutes, 20 pts per question correct, 0 pts per incorrect/skipped) (Short Answer) (range from MC States - MC National)

$\cdot$ History of Math Round - (15 questions, 30 minutes, 5 pts per question, -1 pts per incorrect, 0 pts per skipped) (range from Regional History Bee to National History Bee)

$\cdot$ AoPSTIME! (Art of Problem Solving Talent Identification Mathematical Examination) Round - (5 questions, 40 minutes, weighted by difficulty) (range from AMC 12 Problem 25 to AIME Problem 7)

$\cdot$ Power Round - (3 questions with parts, 1 hour, weighted by difficulty) (range from AIME Problem 8 - USAMO Problem 1.)



The highest score attainable is 558, but if you get around 110, you should be proud, since this can be difficult for those who have not been exposed to proof-based questions, AIME questions, or even history questions.



RULES

1. Do not release any information about the competition content anywhere, including but not limited to social media like Facebook, Twitter, or Instagram. If such content is found, this will result in an automatic ban from any AAMC forum or annual competition.

2. Please wait until the results are out to discuss questions.

3. Please submit your answers via our website to ensure your submission. If you are not sure about anything, feel free to contact reddragon644 by AoPS private messaging or at his e-mail: aops.reddragon644@gmail.com.

4. Have fun!

5. Make sure to follow the past 4 steps!



For more information, please refer to the informational booklet in the link below:

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1YGQtafACKdUMu-IRdaKhSZ9xQm4hc1tPJ8P8j_yIyc8/edit?usp=sharing



or the website of the competition: http://aopsm.weebly.com/instructions.html



The tentative deadline is November 30, 2017, and users will be constantly reminded of the due date through private message.

Reported Errors$\cdot$ The penalty of History of Math Round said -1 on the instructions in the website, but it said 0 on the form, causing confusion. This problem was solved, changing the penalty to 0.




The AAMC ID is created by the participant through registration.



Special thanks to my problem writing group for making this possible!

topics.title: Random question I made up
topics.text: According to Rick Riordan's The Lost Hero, a "nightmare is a bad dream where you can't wake up". If there are 3 ways to get a bad dream, 6 ways to get a good dream, and 10 ways to get a nightmare, what's the probability you get a nightmare and a bad dream in the same night? Assume the dreams are chosen "without replacement" and that you can have only 2 dreams in one night. The nightmare has to be after the bad dream (because otherwise the quote won't do anything).

topics.title: k 0.(9) really equals 1
topics.text:
0.999... repeating, or 0.(9) actually equals 1. The same with any decimal ending in (9): it always equals the directely previous number in the decimal, plus 1. 5.3(9)... = 5.4. 156.7(9)... repeating = 156.8.



This is true because what do you have to add to 0.(9) to get 1? 0.(0)1, but since the 1 is at the end of an infinite number of 0's, you never get to it, so 0.(0)1 is really just 0. Get it?

topics.title: Need help
topics.text:
Every side of an equilateral triangle is divided up into n equal segments. Line segments, parallel to the sides of the triangle, are drawn through each dividing point. The result is that the triangle is sectioned into n^2 mini-triangles. A sequence of mini-triangles that contains no mini-triangle twice, and in which each subsequent mini-triangle shares a side with the previous one is called a "chain." What is the largest possible number of mini-triangles in a chain?



Thanks in advance!

Greetings.I am a year 7 student from Australia and i'm new to AoPS. At school i'm doing a maths competition knows as the APSMO(Australasian Problem Solving Maths Olympiad).Below are some problems for you to solve for fun:

Q1.

Find the whole number value of N so that 3N^2 is closest in value to 2017 solution24


Q2

The mean of 20,x,37,15, and 24 is x.

Find the value of x. solution26


Q3.

Two different numbers are elected from the single digit numbers 1,3,5, and 7 to form a 2-digit number.

How many of these are prime? solution7


Q4.

Find the sum of all the whole numbers N for which exactly three of the four statements below are true:

(1) N is prime.

(2) N - 1 is prime.

(3) 2 < $\sqrt(N)$ < 4.

(4) N is 2 less than a perfect square.

solution7+14=21

topics.title: k Posting and LaTeX
topics.text:
Hey guys, it's me: dragon78! You've probably seen me around... I've been quite active on the forums.

From personal experience, I've had trouble with writing my posts, like using quotes, $\LaTeX$, and hide. Now this post is just to show to all the people out there that aren't sure how to use the tools:



Hide:

[code]

What you want to nameWhat you want to hide
[/code] This gives you: What you want to nameWhat you want to hide




Quotes:

[code][quote=Who you want to quote] What you're quoting [/quote][/code] This gives you: [quote=Who you want to quote]What you're quoting[/quote]



Bolding:

[code]What you want to bold[/code] This gives you: What you want to bold



Underlining:

[code]What you want to underline[/code] This gives you: What you want to underline



Italic Text:

[code]What you want to italisize[/code] This gives you: What you want to italisize



Strike Through:

[code]What you want to put a line through / strike through[/code] This gives you: What you want to put a line through / strike through



Colors and Text Size



For colors highlight what you want to change the color. Then go to the top and you'll find the letter $T$ with a $3$ x $3$ square filled with different colors. Click it, and then pick the colors you'd like. Or you could do: [code][/code] which will give you the color yellow. Change the code in order to change the color.  For text, you'll find the letter $T$ three times, growing from small to big. Click that, and then click the size you would like. You could also do: [code]hi[/code]



$\LaTeX$:



First off check out this: https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php?title=LaTeX:LaTeX_on_AoPS It will help you a lot.



To practice your $\LaTeX$ go to this forum: https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c68_



IF YOU WOULD LIKE TO USE $\LaTeX$ YOU CAN ALSO POST ON THIS THREAD FOR PRACTICE



The Basics:



It's pretty simple. All you do is put a dollar sign before and after of what you want to be $\LaTeX$.

Angle sign: [code]$\angle ABC$[/code] This gives you: $\angle ABC$



Degree: [code]$90^\circ$[/code] This gives you: $90^\circ$



Equation(Power): [code]$a^2+b^2>c^2$[/code]

This gives you: $a^2+b^2>c^2$.

The "^" sign is to raise something to the power. The ">" or "<" sign can be used by just doing [code]$>$ and $<$[/code]



Greater than or Equal to Sign: [code]$\ge$[/code] This gives you: $\ge$



Less than or Equal to Sign: [code]$\le$[/code] This gives you: $\le$



Triangle: [code]$\triangle ABC$[/code] This gives you: $\triangle ABC$



To write $\LaTeX$, do: [code]$\LaTeX$[/code] (P.S.) you can also do: [code]$\text{\LaTeX}$[/code] Which will give you: $\text{\LaTeX}$.



Pi: [code]$\pi$[/code] This gives you: $\pi$



Phi: [code]$\phi$[/code] This gives you: $\phi$



Square Root: [code]$\sqrt{39}$[/code] This gives you: $\sqrt{39}$



More to Roots: [code]$\sqrt[3]{5}$[/code] This gives you: $\sqrt[3]{5}$



Fractions: [code]$\frac{1}{2}$[/code] This gives you: $\frac{1}{2}$



Summation: [code]$\sum$[/code] This gives you: $\sum$

But... just wanting the summation sign doesn't help us much...

So let's try this: [code]$\sum\limits_{n=1}^{+\infty } \frac{1}{n}$[/code] This gives you: $\sum\limits_{n=1}^{+\infty } \frac{1}{n}$



Factorial: [code]$n!$[/code] This gives you: $n!$



Integrals: [code]$\int$[/code] This gives you: $\int$ (I will be giving a farther explanation for this later)



Right Arrow: [code]$\to$[/code] This gives you: $\to$



Infinity Sign: [code]$\infty$[/code] This gives you: $\infty$



Limits: [code]$\lim_{n\to\infty}$[/code] This gives you: $\lim_{n\to\infty}$



With the top three (Integrals, Right Arrow, and Infinity Sign) You can do something like this: [code]$\lim_{x\to\infty}$[/code] This would give you: $\lim_{x\to\infty}$



Approximate Sign: [code]$9.9 \approx 10$[/code] This gives you: $9.9 \approx 10$



Boxing: [code]$\boxed {n}$[/code] This gives you: $\boxed {n}$



Square: [code]$\square$[/code] This gives you: $\square$



Plus or Minus: [code]$\pm$[/code] This gives you: $\pm$



BTW Asymptote will be coming soon! (As in on this post)  ;)  :play_ball:



:sleeping:  :sleep2: Whew that was REALLY  tiring to write. :P



I will add more to this post as much as possible for others to learn off from it! Thank you for the likes! I will try my best! :) Remember there's a lot more to posting and $\LaTeX$. These are just the basics! I will be adding more and more! Please tell or alert me if I have a typo or mistake. That would be really helpful! Thanks again! (Please, no spam :spam: , and moderators please don't lock this.)  :read:

topics.title: k Mirror Problem
topics.text:
This Problem is created by cookiemonster2004. Don't waste your time searching on Google because there won't be any solutions. Have fun! This is a great learning opportunity for you people that over complicate problems.

ProblemOn the left side of the room, there is one photon. On the right side of the room, there is a light detector (photon is a light particle). The photon will travel the shortest path possible toward the light detector if there is no interference. However, between the photon and the light detector, there are 2047 "magical" mirrors. The mirrors are magical because whenever the photon hits any mirror, it has $\frac{1}{2}$ chance of passing through, and $\frac{1}{2}$ chance of being reflected, independent of the previous times it has hit the mirror and the times it has hit any other mirror. Also, there is no gravity. In addition, the photon is destroyed if it hits a wall, located to the left of the photon's starting position. What is the probability that the light detector will detect the photon? Express your answer as a common fraction.


For You People Picky About detailFor you people who are picky about detail:

1. The faces of the mirrors are all parallel to each other, and the faces of the mirrors are perpendicular to the trajectory of the photon.

2. No air resistance, friction, etc. etc.

3. Yes, the detector can ACTUALLY detect the photon (if the photon ever hit the detector)

4. No, the photon can't "miss" the detector (if it passes through the 2047th mirror)

5. Everything is in a vacuum. (So the photon won't change its course due to the air or something)

6. The 1/2 chance of bouncing back/passing through is TRUE RANDOM, not generated random.


DiagramHere's a diagram of the problem

|

|          $\qquad$ O $\qquad$            |   |   |   |   ....  |     Detector

|

The "|" on the very left side is the wall.

The "O" is the photon.

The "|"s to the right of the "O" are the mirrors

To the right of the mirrors is the detector.


If you think you've solved the problem, please PM me the solution, do not post any hints/partial solutions in the post (don't spoil it for other people)



(And no, the answer is NOT $\frac{1}{2^{2047}}$)



Have fun! :D



(Do not scroll down if you want to solve the problem by yourself. There might be spoilers/hints even though I specifically asked for no hints)

topics.title: For Those Moving On
topics.text:
Hello AoPs community,IntroductionThe school year of 2017-2018 is close to finishing. So many 8th graders have went to Mathcounts Nationals for their last time. There are 16 6th graders and 11 repeat 7th graders, which means there are over 150 8th graders who are now wondering what to do with their math lives. Congratulations to everyone for your success this math year. I can only guess how many students dream to see Mr. Aops founder (Sorry, I have always misspelled your name even though we have had talks each year) or eat a chocolate calculator or go to Washington, D.C. If you are reading this, you are probably an 8th grader whose Middle School Math journey is about to end. There are many users that have touched your lives in AoPs, so please come back to this forum regularly to touch the younger ones on their math journey's and make it worthwhile. As I said in the Three-Timers Video, try your hardest because that is the only thing that will not make you feel like you did not do your best. I know that sometimes, things just don't go as planned. Sometimes you just know that you could have done better. At that moment, realize that its not the end of the world. Realize that you have achieved something special, and that your result, poor or outstanding, may not be an accurate representation of yourself. If you know that you are better than what you did, then just try harder next year. Don't let this experience be a traumatic moment for you. Let it build you up. I know how much Mathcounts means, and it will be so hard for me to let it go. Mathcounts is a huge experience that was one of the things that brought me out of this shell. There are times where you just don't think about how blessed you really are. There were homeless people on the streets while you were eating. There were only 224 Mathcounts national people. There were less than 12 people in Middle School who have the Team Spirit Award Pin. Less than 5% make AIME. So what if you are from a "bad state." I'm from Louisiana. We tried our hardest and got 36th team. So what if you are in Algebra 1 or not even in Prealgebra. I won 1st in state before taking Prealgebra in 6th grade and in 8th grade when taking Algebra 1. So what if you are 26th in chapter because you have tough competition. My friend when back from that and then beat me at Nationals. So what if you don't make school team? Look at the people that are flabbergasted that they still made Mathcounts Nationals. So what if you are homeschooled? Look at Luke. So what if your Middle School Career is over? So what if you choked on countdown and you got to be a moderator of Middle School Math and can delete this at any time? (*cough* Reagan). So what if 7th graders are better than you? (*cough me) So what if you didn't do as well as last year? Take a moment to thank AoPs and Mathcounts and your teachers and parents and everyone else.



Just try your best because your math journey didn't end, but it has just begun.




So what? (Resources)Yeah, yeah, yeah. That was corny-ish. So what? It's true. Touch those fellow math nerds to do what you did. There are so many people that look up to you. Just being in AoPs makes you part of the family. If you have actually read all of this, thank you for spending some time. For those who just scrolled down to here, lol. That sounds like something I would have done in 6th grade. There are many competitions that are available in high school.High School:

AMC 10/12 -> AIME -> USA(J)MO

ARML (American Regions Math League)

HMMT (Harvard-MIT)

Math Prize for girls

Purple Comet

USA Mathematical Talent Search

Who Wants to Be a Mathematician

...etc (MathKangaroo, Academic Games, BMT (Berkeley Math Tournament), etc.)
 There are also many Summer Programs available. This was mostly from the "After MATHCOUNTS Resources List" provided by AoPs at the breakfast before the competitors left in Mathcounts Nationals.




Thank you and Conclusion and OtherThank you for your time for reading this long post, no matter how difficult it was to read. Those of you who have aso breached upon the same topic, please post resources and advice down below. I will try to add it to the original post with your username as credits by it so that there is a thread dedicated For Those Moving On





Additional Advice Given in the Thread[quote=mathwizard888]

Don't stress over the past[/quote]




Please do not spam or post unless you are giving advice.



Please read this post and the Basic Forum Rules before you post on this thread

topics.title: k Stuff about national cutoffs
topics.text:
I don't really know where to post this, and it honestly may be too late now, but I feel like it's important enough for me to post it somewhere. Since this is where most of the "post-state MathCounts salt" is at, I'll post it here.



Recently, I've been bothered a lot by a certain type of post that seems to be recurring on a bunch of these MathCounts threads. Here are a few of them (not direct quotes):



[quote=Some annoyed user]Wait, the Wyoming national cutoff was 18??? Omg, why can't I move there! I'm moving to Wyoming now![/quote]



[quote=A meme]Wait, a 33 won state in Nebraska??? I would have easily won state if I lived there!!![/quote]



Can people stop making these types of jokes? As someone who lives in a state is pretty bad at math in general, I can guarantee that if you actually moved to Wyoming, or any state with a marginally low nationals cutoff, from a state with a much higher cutoff, you wouldn't be incredibly happy with living there, especially if you're someone who enjoys math. Over here in Nebraska, we don't even have the ability to go to competitions like HMMT and PUMaC due to a lack of interest. The same goes for MathCounts. I only know of one school that practices more than once a week, which seems to be a norm in many other places that are somewhat competitive. Would you like to live in a place that lacks so many opportunities?



Considering the lack of resources, popularity of math, and even the lack of people in itself: 18 isn't too shabby for a nationals cutoff, even in comparison to a math-powerhouse like Texas, which has nearly 50 times the amount of people. I can assure you that you would be marginally worse at math if you were someone who had lived in Wyoming your whole life, as opposed to someone who had lived in Caliornia their whole life. There would even be a decently high chance that you would never know of the existence of math competitions, period.



Also, from personal experience, I can definitely say that it doesn't feel good at all when people ridicule the national cutoff of your state; because it truly makes you believe that your qualification was undeserved, resulting in a lot of guilty feelings. These are the exact feelings I felt last year when I revealed to the community that I had won my state competition with a 33, which I was bashed at for quite a bit. Consequently, those feelings came with a lot of perceived pressure that I had to prove myself at nationals, which ultimately ended with me breaking down and performing the worst that I ever have at a competition so far.



So a) please refrain from making these types of jokes on the fora and b) please be a little bit more considerate of people who may be less fortunate than you because they happen to live in rural areas. Instead, wherever you are, focus on improving and maximizing your success, because if you live in a fairly populous area, you probably have a lot of room for it.



Thanks,

le qk

topics.text:
The sequence $0, 1, 1, 1, ..., 1$ contains $1996$ numbers, the first being zero and all the others equal to $1$. Two or more numbers are chosen from the sequence (but not the entire sequence) and one of them is replaced by the arithmetic mean of the numbers chosen, thus obtaining a new sequence of $1996$ numbers. Prove that, with the repetition of this operation, it is possible to obtain a sequence in which the $1996$ numbers are equal.

NOTE: In each operation you do not necessarily have to choose the same number of numbers.
